messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Librarian
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mai was 52 when she finally agreed to seek help, after months of living as if she had to keep one part of herself on watch at all times. She was born in the United States to South Eastern Asian parents, and had spent most of her adult life in the same quiet suburban town with her husband. She worked as a librarian, a job she had once loved for its order and calm, though in recent months even the hush of the building had become complicated for her. In the library, she found herself choosing seats with unusual care, always looking first for the wall behind her, the clearest view of the doors, the place where she could feel most protected. If a room fell suddenly silent, or if she walked into a darker aisle after the overhead lights had been dimmed, her body would tense before she could think. At those moments she became intensely watchful, scanning the space automatically, checking who was near her and where she might go if something felt wrong.

The trauma had occurred years earlier during a powerful natural disaster that struck without warning in the middle of the night. Mai had been asleep with her husband when the world outside seemed to break apart all at once. What stayed with her was not only the violence of the event but the abrupt darkness and the unnerving stillness that followed in between bursts of sound. In the confusion, people around her were shouting, running, and trying to reach one another, and she later found that anything reminding her of those close human links to the disaster could pull her back into it with startling force. Hearing someone talk about families affected by the storm, or seeing people connected in any way to the event, could make her chest tighten and her mind flash straight back to that night. The recollection was not something she summoned carefully; it could seize her when she least expected it, arriving full and immediate from a sound, a phrase, or a moment of silence around her.

Over time, Mai began to dread the conditions that most resembled the disaster. Night-time was particularly hard. Waking in the dark could send a jolt through her, as if she had been returned to the instant when she could not see what was happening beyond the windows. She started avoiding being in dark circumstances whenever she could, keeping lights on in the house longer than before and hesitating before entering dim places. In the library, she sometimes asked for different tasks rather than entering the lower-lit storage rooms, and she noticed that she spent more energy arranging herself around safety than she used to. Even simple pauses in conversation could unsettle her; a sudden complete silence in the house, or in a room at work, could bring the event back with such force that she felt thrown into it rather than merely reminded of it. When that happened, she would sometimes deliberately try to leave her body or blank out, wanting nothing more than to escape the intensity of what had risen in her mind and senses. She described it as trying to disappear from herself for a few moments, because facing the memory directly felt unbearable.

What troubled her most about remembering was the grief that came with it. When the memory forced its way in, she did not only feel fear; she was also overwhelmed by sorrow for what had been lost in that night and in the aftermath. She could be standing at the circulation desk, checking books in, when a comment from a patron or the sudden quiet of the afternoon would bring the scene back without warning, and she would have to fight to keep her face composed. The memory did not wait for her permission. It intruded while she was working, while she was at home, and sometimes while she was trying to rest, leaving her exhausted by the effort of containing it. She had also stopped exercising, something she once used to clear her head, because moving her body too much seemed to make her feel exposed and vulnerable in ways she could not tolerate. Her avoidance had gradually narrowed her routine, and her husband noticed that she was less willing to go out after dark and more inclined to sit quietly in places where she could monitor the room.

By the time she came for treatment, Mai was tired of living so narrowly, but she was also afraid of what might happen if she let her guard down. She did not want to keep being superalert, constantly scanning every room, but she was not yet sure how to feel safe otherwise. What finally brought her in was the sense that the memory was taking over too often — that it could come rushing back without warning in the library, at home, or in the dark, carrying the same grief and terror she had felt before. She hoped for relief from the sudden intrusions and for a way to sleep through the night without dreading the dark, while fearing most that if she stopped watching so carefully, something terrible would happen again.
